insider_note: Writing sec²x·csc²x as 1/(cos²x sin²x) and then splitting the numerator 1 into sin²x+cos²x is the standard trick for a product of two reciprocal-squared trig functions.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rewrite using sin²x + cos²x = 1
steps.why: Replacing the numerator 1 with sin²x+cos²x (always true) and splitting the fraction turns one product into a sum of two separately-integrable standard terms.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate sec²x·cosec²x as a product directly, with no standard rule for that combination.
Splitting the fraction incorrectly, e.g. as sinx/cosx + cosx/sinx.
steps.memory_tip: 1 = sin²x+cos²x is the single move that turns this product into a sum — use it whenever a bare 1 could help split a fraction.

steps.label: Split and integrate for the final answer
steps.why: ∫sec²x dx = tanx and ∫cosec²x dx = −cotx are both standard derivatives, so the split sum integrates term by term immediately.
common_mistakes: Writing +cotx instead of −cotx — ∫cosec²x dx is −cotx, not +cotx.
steps.memory_tip: ∫sec²x=tanx (plus); ∫cosec²x=−cotx (minus) — opposite signs, easy to mix up.
